ety.text: From Middle English livynge, libbyng, livinde, livand, livende, libbinde, libbende, from Old English lifiġende, lifiende, libbende, from Proto-West Germanic *libbjandī, from Proto-Germanic *libjandz (“living”), present participle of Proto-Germanic *libjaną (“to live”), equivalent to live + -ing. Cognate with West Frisian libbend (“living”), Dutch levend (“living”), German lebend (“living”), Swedish levande (“living”), Icelandic lifandi (“living”).
From Middle English livynge, libbynge, equivalent to live + -ing. Cognate with Middle Dutch levinge, (whence Dutch leving (“way of life, living”)), Middle Low German lēvinge (“living”).

senses.d: Having life; alive.
ex: a living, breathing child
Respect for the dead does not preclude respect for the living.

senses.d: In use or existing.
ex: Hunanese is a living language.

senses.d: True to life.
ex: This is the living image of Fidel Castro.

senses.d: Of rock or stone, existing in its original state and place.
Continually updated; not static
ex: HTML is a living standard.

senses.d: Used as an intensifier.
ex: He almost beat the living daylights out of me.

senses.d: The state of being alive.
Financial means; a means of maintaining life; livelihood
ex: it's a living
What do you do for a living?

senses.d: A style of life.
ex: plain living
The National Brewing Company declared that the Chesapeake Bay region was the Land of Pleasant Living.

senses.d: Those who are alive: living people.
ex: in the land of the living
Glad to see you're still among the living! [good-humored greeting]

senses.d: A position in a church (usually the Church of England) that has attached to it a source of income; an ecclesiastical benefice.

ety.text: From Middle English lyvere, lyver, from Old English lifer (“liver”), from Proto-West Germanic *libru, from Proto-Germanic *librō, from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to smear, smudge, stick”), from Proto-Indo-European *ley- (“to be slimy, be sticky, glide”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Líeuwer, Lieuwer (“liver”),German Leber (“liver”), Danish, Dutch, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, Swedish, and West Frisian lever (“liver”), Faroese livur (“liver”), Icelandic lifur (“liver”). Related to live.
From Middle English lyvere, livere, equivalent to live + -er.

senses.d: A large organ in the body that stores and metabolizes nutrients, destroys toxins and produces bile. It is responsible for thousands of biochemical reactions.
ex: Steve Jobs is a famous liver transplant recipient.

senses.d: This organ, as taken from animals used as food.
ex: I'd like some goose liver pate.
You could fry up some chicken livers for a tasty treat. — Nah, I don't like chicken liver.

senses.d: A dark brown colour, tinted with red and gray, like the colour of liver.
Any of various chemical compounds—particularly sulfides—thought to resemble livers in color.
ex: He gave his horse some liver of antimony.

senses.d: Of the colour of liver (dark brown, tinted with red and gray).
ex: His friend Rothwell, who had the use of the best Laveracks for breeding purposes, wrote him that one of his puppies was liver and white.

senses.d: Someone who lives (usually in a specified way).
ex: a wicked liver may be reclaimed, and prove an honest man[…].
Try if life be worth the liver's care.

senses.d: Someone who is alive: one of the living.
ex: Thou king of heaven, which […] Dost see the secret of each livers heart.
When as the wandring Scots and Picthts King Marius had subdude, He gave the Liuers dwellings.

senses.d: Someone who lives in a particular place; an inhabitant, a dweller.
ex: They must instantly have been detected by the present Livers that were upon the place.
One, John Powle, a Liver on Sasquehanna River.

ety.text: Inherited from Old French foie, feie, from Late Latin fīcātum (“liver (as food)”), from Latin iecur fīcātum (“fig-stuffed liver, foie gras”). The French form goes back to a byform ficatum with a short accented -i- (whence Italian fegato), which was then metathesised to *fitacum.

it:fegato.gl: liver (organ of human or animal; organ of animal used as food)

An apheretic form of alive.

senses.d: To be alive; to have life.
ex: He's not expected to live for more than a few months.

senses.d: To have permanent residence somewhere, to inhabit, to reside.
ex: I live at 2a Acacia Avenue.  At that time I'd been living in a camper for about six months.

senses.d: (of an object) to have its proper place; to normally be stored.
ex: I washed your gravy boat. Where does it live?

senses.d: To survive; to persevere; to continue.
To endure in memory; to escape oblivion.
ex: Her memory lives in that song.

senses.d: To cope.
ex: You'll just have to live with it!  I can't live in a world without you.

senses.d: To pass life in a specified manner.
ex: It is difficult to live in poverty.   And they lived happily ever after.

senses.d: To spend, as one's life; to pass; to maintain; to continue in, constantly or habitually.
ex: To live an idle or a useful life.
Many people write their romances, others live them; Honore de Balzac did both.

senses.d: To act habitually in conformity with; to practice; to exemplify in one's way of life.
ex: to live the Gospel
The key to our freedom then, isn't begging for tolerance, but living our full rights.

senses.d: To live as; to live being.
ex:
at leaſt admit vs libertie,
Euen as thou hopſt to be eternized,
By liuing Aſias mightie Emperour.

senses.d: Having life; that is alive.
ex: The post office will not ship live animals.

senses.d: Being in existence; actual.
ex: He is a live example of the consequences of excessive drinking.

senses.d: Having active properties; being energized.
ex: Because the vaccinia virus is live, it is important to follow care instructions for the vaccination site.

senses.d: Operational; in actual use rather than in testing etc.
Of an object or value: that may potentially be used in the future execution of a program.
ex: An object in the heap is live if its address is held in a root, or there is a pointer to it held in another live heap node.

senses.d: Taken from a living animal.
ex: live feathers

senses.d: Imparting power; having motion.
ex: the live spindle of a lathe
a live, or driving, axle

senses.d: Still in active play.
ex: a live ball

senses.d: Of a card: not yet dealt or played.
Being broadcast (“on the air”), as it happens.
ex: The station presented a live news program every evening.
Are we live?

senses.d: Of an event, as it happens; in real time; direct.
ex: The concert was broadcast live by radio.

senses.d: Of making a performance or speech, in person.
ex: He'll be appearing live at the auditorium.

grp.label: (broadcasting) seen or heard from a broadcast, as it happens

senses.d: Full of life; energetic, vivacious.
ex: But wherefore comes old Manoa in such haſt, / With youthful ſteps? much livelier then e're while / He ſeems.

senses.d: Bright, glowing, vivid; strong, vigorous.
ex: The colours of the prism are manifestly more full, intense, and lively that those of natural bodies.

senses.d: Endowed with or manifesting life; living.
ex:
c. 1600, Philemon Holland
chaplets of gold and silver resembling lively flowers and leaves

senses.d: Representing life; lifelike.
ex: I spied the lively picture of my father.

senses.d: Airy; animated; spirited.
ex: From grave to gay, from lively to ſevere, [...]

senses.d: Fizzy; foamy; tending to produce a large head in the glass.

senses.d: Vigorously.
Vibrantly, vividly.
In a lifelike manner.
